keyVerseText: Which also were accounted giants, as the Anakims; but the Moabites call them Emims.
rootMeaning: The root word מוֹאָב (Môwʼâb) literally means "of his father," referring to Moab, the son of Lot by his eldest daughter. This patronymic origin highlights a complex and somber family history, as Moab was born out of an incestuous relationship. The feminine form מוֹאָבִי (Môwʼâbîy) or מוֹאָבִיָּה (Môwʼâbîyâh) specifically denotes a Moabite woman, emphasizing descent from this patriarchal line. This etymology enriches the common English gloss by connecting the identity of the Moabites to their ancestral origin and the narrative of their founder.
usageInScripture: The term מוֹאָבִי (Môwʼâbîy) occurs 16 times in Scripture, predominantly translated as "the Moabitess" five times, highlighting the frequent mention of Moabite women in the biblical text. It appears also as a masculine noun and collective plural referring to the people of Moab, indicating both individual and communal identities. The consistent use of the term to denote descendants or inhabitants of Moab reveals a clear ethnic and geographical identity rooted in the biblical narrative. This usage underscores the Moabites’ distinct place among the neighboring peoples of Israel.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מוֹאָבִי (Môwʼâbîy) as a term deeply tied to lineage and origin invites reflection on God's dealings with nations and peoples rooted in complex histories. The Moabites, descended from Lot's incestuous son, represent both the consequences of human sin and the broader scope of God's redemptive plan that includes even those with difficult beginnings. Recognizing the Moabite identity reminds believers of the sovereignty of God over all nations and the call to faithfulness despite ancestral or cultural backgrounds. It also points to the importance of faith and covenant over ethnicity alone, as seen in biblical narratives involving Moabite individuals who come to faith.
keyVerseReflection: Deuteronomy 2:11 notes that the Moabites called certain giants "Emims," paralleling the Anakims. The mention of Moabites here not only locates these people geographically and ethnically but also associates them with a formidable heritage and a land inhabited by giants. The term מוֹאָבִי underscores the identity of these people as descendants of Moab, framing their historical and spiritual context within the biblical narrative. This highlights the ongoing tension and interaction between Israel and the Moabites in God's unfolding plan.
